bib.title: No More Manual Tests? Evaluating and Improving ChatGPT for Unit Test Generation
bib.venue: Proc. ACM Softw. Eng. 1, FSE, Article 76 (arXiv v3 of 2305.04207)

question: How correct, sufficient, readable and usable are unit tests generated by ChatGPT, and can feeding compiler errors and an intention step back to ChatGPT improve them?
hypothesis: Most compile errors come from missing deep code knowledge and most execution failures from misunderstood method intention; fixing each (iterative compile-error repair, intention prompt) should improve correctness.
contributions: First study of correctness, sufficiency, readability and usability of ChatGPT-generated tests via quantitative analysis and user study
Findings and practical implications on limits and prospects
ChatTester: initial test generator (intention then generation prompt) plus iterative test refiner
Evaluation showing effectiveness and generalisation to two open-source LLMs

method.summary: Builds a benchmark of 1,000 Java focal methods with executable Maven projects, queries gpt-3.5-turbo with a zero-shot prompt and measures compile, pass, coverage and a 5-person readability/usability study. Then proposes ChatTester: an intention prompt before generation, plus a compile-validate-fix loop that adds error type, buggy line and related class signatures, stopping on success or after more than 3 non-improving rounds.

datasets.name: Study benchmark (from CodeSearchNet Java projects)
datasets.size: 1,000 focal-method/test pairs from 185 Maven Java projects (502/118 code/test files, 244,876/20,934 LOC)
datasets.source: CodeSearchNet 4,685 projects filtered: updated by 2023-01-01, >=100 stars, Maven and compilable; cloned 2023-03-25
datasets.preprocessing: Pairs by @Test method and file-path/class-name matching; only single-test-case methods kept

other.note: GPT-4 not used due to API rate limits

models.name: AthenaTest (reproduced with CodeT5)
models.init_from: CodeT5, fine-tuned on AthenaTest fine-tuning data with overlap with benchmark removed

inference.samples: Study: one run, not repeated. ChatTester evaluation: all experiments repeated three times, average reported.
inference.prompting: Zero-shot. Basic prompt: role line plus task line plus code context (focal method, class name, fields, signatures of all class methods). ChatTester: intention prompt then generation prompt including the intention; refiner prompt with error type, <Buggy line> tag, buggy element and extracted class declaration plus public method signatures.
inference.retrieval: Code analyzer parses whole project to find the class of the buggy element and adds its declaration and public method signatures.

parameters.stop: compiles, or accumulated invalid refinements exceed max; invalid = error count >= previous round
parameters.scope: fixes compile errors only, not execution errors

other.temperature_note: temperature, top_p and max tokens not stated

metrics.name: statement / branch coverage
metrics.definition: Jacoco coverage on focal method (study) or whole project (RQ7)

eval.protocol: User study: five Java developers (4 to 5 years experience), 248 passing ChatGPT tests vs paired manual tests, blind, 250$ reward each, two weeks. Project-level: 219 tests per technique (0.05 margin, 95% confidence). Failed tests manually checked for focal-method bugs.

prompts.text: You are a professional who writes Java test methods.
Please write a test method for the {focal method name} based on the given information using {Junit version}

evidence.quote: the accumulated number of invalid refinements is larger than the maximum (e.g., 3 in our experiments)

results.claim: With the basic prompt only 42.1% of ChatGPT tests compile and 24.8% pass execution.
results.setup: 1,000 Java focal methods from 185 Maven projects; gpt-3.5-turbo, default API settings, basic zero-shot prompt; one run; test placed in focal class directory then compiled and run
results.quote: 42.1% of the generated tests are successfully compiled while only 24.8% of the generated tests are executed successfully without any execution errors

results.claim: Compilation rate of basic ChatGPT prompt on the 1,000-method study set.
results.setup: 1,000 Java focal methods from 185 Maven projects; gpt-3.5-turbo, default API settings, basic zero-shot prompt; one run; test placed in focal class directory then compiled and run
results.table: Table 2, row Success compilation, column ChatGPT

results.claim: 57.9% of ChatGPT tests fail to compile and 17.3% compile but fail at execution.
results.setup: 1,000 Java focal methods from 185 Maven projects; gpt-3.5-turbo, default API settings, basic zero-shot prompt; one run; test placed in focal class directory then compiled and run
results.note: Table 2 gives 42.1% compiled; 579 uncompilable tests in Table 3 text; 17.3% = 173 failing executions summed from Table 4 (148+6+5+3+11), derived
results.quote: 57.9% of ChatGPT-generated tests encounter compilation errors

results.claim: 85.5% of failed executions are assertion errors, and manual inspection found all were incorrect assertions, not focal-method bugs.
results.setup: 1,000 Java focal methods from 185 Maven projects; gpt-3.5-turbo, default API settings, basic zero-shot prompt; one run; test placed in focal class directory then compiled and run; Table 4 counts: 148 assertion errors of 173 failed executions
results.quote: the majority of failed executions (85.5%) are caused by assertion errors

results.claim: Most compile errors are unresolved symbols; 'cannot find symbol class' occurs 1,934 times across 579 uncompilable tests.
results.setup: 1,000 Java focal methods from 185 Maven projects; gpt-3.5-turbo, default API settings, basic zero-shot prompt; one run; test placed in focal class directory then compiled and run; multiple errors per test possible
results.table: Table 3, row Cannot find symbol class, column Frequency

results.claim: Passing ChatGPT tests reach statement coverage 82.3% vs 84.2% for manual tests (branch 65.6 vs 68.9).
results.setup: Focal methods where both ChatGPT and Evosuite produce executable tests; Jacoco; coverage on focal method

results.claim: Full ChatTester raises compilation from 39.0% to 73.3% (+34.3 points).
results.setup: 100 held-out Java focal methods (from remaining 748 pairs); gpt-3.5-turbo; average of three runs
results.quote: additional 34.3% tests (= 73.3% - 39.0%) can be successfully compiled

results.claim: Full ChatTester raises passing execution from 22.3% to 41.0% (+18.7 points).
results.setup: 100 held-out Java focal methods (from remaining 748 pairs); gpt-3.5-turbo; average of three runs
results.quote: additional 18.7% tests (= 41.0% - 22.3%) can pass the execution

results.claim: Iterative refiner alone (ChatTester-Ini, no intention prompt) lifts compilation to 60.6% and passing to 34.0%.
results.setup: 100 held-out Java focal methods (from remaining 748 pairs); gpt-3.5-turbo; average of three runs; refiner: compile, parse error, add buggy line and class context, up to 3 invalid refinements
results.note: Passing 34.0 (Table 7, row Passing execution, column ChatTester-Ini) vs 22.3 baseline
results.table: Table 7, row Success compilation, column ChatTester-Ini

results.claim: Intention-first generator alone (ChatTester-Ite) gives 50.7% compile and 29.7% pass.
results.setup: 100 held-out Java focal methods (from remaining 748 pairs); gpt-3.5-turbo; average of three runs
results.note: Compilation 50.7; text: 11.7% and 7.4% improvements; 12.5% of incorrect assertions fixed
results.table: Table 7, row Passing execution, column ChatTester-Ite

results.claim: Adding the refiner to the intention prompt fixes an extra 22.6% compilable and 11.3% passing tests.
results.setup: 100 held-out Java focal methods (from remaining 748 pairs); gpt-3.5-turbo; average of three runs
results.quote: additional 22.6% tests and 11.3% tests are fixed by the iterative test refiner into compilable tests and passing tests

results.claim: Average ChatTester cost is about 99.0 seconds per focal method: 15.0 s initial generator plus about 30.0 s per refiner iteration.
results.setup: 100 held-out Java focal methods (from remaining 748 pairs); gpt-3.5-turbo; average of three runs
results.quote: The average time cost of ChatTester is around 99.0 seconds, where the initial test generator takes 15.0 seconds while each iteration in the iterative refiner takes 30.0 seconds on average

results.claim: Tests that needed late refinement (iterations 5 to 7) compiled but none passed execution.
results.setup: 100 held-out Java focal methods (from remaining 748 pairs); gpt-3.5-turbo; average of three runs
results.table: Table 8, row Passing Execution, columns 5 to 7

results.claim: ChatTester lifts CodeLlama-Instruct-34B passing from 3.0% to 21.0% and CodeFuse-34B from 0.0% to 11.0%.
results.setup: 100 held-out Java focal methods (from remaining 748 pairs); gpt-3.5-turbo; average of three runs; CodeLlama-Instruct-34B and CodeFuse-34B replace ChatGPT
results.table: Table 9, row Passing execution, column CodeLlama-ChatTester

results.claim: On Python HumanEval (164 methods) ChatTester raises successful execution from 31.7% to 43.2%.
results.quote: improving the successful execution rate of ChatGPT-generated tests from 31.7% to 43.2%

results.claim: Project-level statement coverage on zappos-json: ChatTester 35.1% vs ChatGPT 14.4% and Evosuite 30.5%; on tabula-java and jInstagram results are mixed.
results.setup: Three projects (3,552 to 6,303 LOC), tests for every method
results.note: jInstagram SC: Evosuite 45.3 > ChatTester 41.8; tabula-java BC: Evosuite 9.9 > ChatTester 9.2
results.table: Table 10, row ChatTester, column zappos-json SC

limits: Study run once, not repeated, because of the user-study effort; ChatTester evaluation uses only 100 focal methods averaged over three runs.
Only Java/JUnit with Maven; Python check on HumanEval only.
Refiner fixes compile errors only; execution failures cannot be told apart as bad test vs bad focal method.
gpt-3.5-turbo only, default settings; no temperature or token limits stated; possible training-data leakage (Levenshtein distance check: mean 1,027 chars, median 609; 5% under 200).
Evosuite's higher compile and pass rates come from post-generation validation; authors say not to conclude it is better.
